title: I've been building an autonomous potato civilization sim with AI -- The Last Taters
author: GuideAffectionate901
selftext:
The basic idea is a cozy autonomous civilization sim inside a giant garden box. You play as The Gardener, but you don't directly control the taters. You can influence their world -- build things, protect them, ring the settlement bell, interfere when necessary -- but the taters decide what to do with the world you give them.

It started as a pretty tiny experiment, but I've been using AI heavily as like a partner and it has turned into something much larger than I originally expected.

At this point the taters gather food and resources, build homes and workplaces, plant new spuds, form relationships, develop skills, discover materials, create paths based on actual travel, respond to Zombacon (zombie bacon lol) at night, hold gatherings, develop government and customs, remember important people and events, and gradually turn the garden into a settlement with its own history.

One of the rules I've tried to stick to is that the player can influence the world, but cannot control the taters. A lot of the development work has actually been trying to stop the simulation from feeling scripted while also stopping the AI from doing completely stupid things.

We've spent a ridiculous amount of time on things like population pacing, starvation behavior, housing, autonomous construction, natural path formation, rebuilding destroyed structures, combat behavior, day/night survival, save compatibility, mobile controls, and long-session simulation stability.

The current 0.8 development cycle is less about adding another pile of mechanics and more about making the existing simulation visible.

I recently added a Cinematic Watch mode that acts like a little director. It moves around the settlement and follows whatever seems interesting. It can quietly follow an individual tater going about their day, but it can also interrupt itself when something important happens.

The newest part is a story-card system that tells you why the camera is showing something -- a discovery, a gathering, a little life moment, a death, a Zombacon encounter, etc.

I also just added the first proper opening sequence. A new garden starts empty, gives a short introduction to the Gardener/tater relationship, and then hands control over to you to choose where the First Spud gets planted.

Everything visually is still deliberately pretty simple and mostly code-drawn. The game is HTML5/JavaScript/Canvas and runs in the browser. Mobile is also a major goal -- eventually I'd like it polished enough to package for Android.

Before making this post I ran another little regression/playtest. I simulated four separate gardens out to Day 10. All four survived, but they developed pretty differently. Population ended between 6 and 9 taters, Age II happened anywhere from Day 5 to Day 9, some gardens barely saw Zombacon while another started heavily fortifying itself, and one discovered early ore/material systems while the others hadn't yet.

That kind of variation is what I've been chasing.

There's still a lot I want to improve. Farms need a stronger visual footprint, settlement history needs to physically show up in the world more, audio/music is still early, late-game progression needs a lot more development, and the whole thing needs more visual polish.

I'm curious what stands out to people who haven't watched this thing evolve from the beginning.

Does the "autonomous civilization you influence but don't control" idea sound interesting? And if you were playtesting something like this, what would you be watching for first?

I'm happy to talk about the AI workflow too. A lot of this project has been less "give AI one prompt and get a game" and more using it for, audits, simulation testing, debugging, balancing, and repeatedly tearing apart systems that technically worked but didn't actually feel like a game.
